name: Kerek
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Skorik, P. Ya. 1968, 'Kerekskij jazyk', in Jazyki narodov SSSR vol. 5 (grammar sketch, pp. 310-333); not found online.

new_statements.quote: ...долгота фонологического статуса не имеет. Просодическая организация словоформы подчиняется тем же закономерностям, которые свойственны всем чукотско-корякским языкам (ср. статью «Чукотский язык»). В идиолектах отдельных кереков (более широкие выводы сделать затруднительно) фиксируется мена просодического рисунка словоформы, выражающаяся в том, что долготное выделение получают разные слоги: куниикаӈ 'ты делаешь/он делает' — мэккууникаӈ 'мы (дв.) делаем' — ткуйааникаӈэӈ 'я хочу делать'. Фонологически значимых тонов в К.я. нет.
new_statements.translation: ...length has no phonological status. The prosodic organization of the word form obeys the same regularities that are characteristic of all Chukotko-Koryak languages (cf. the article 'Chukchi language'). In the idiolects of individual Kereks (broader conclusions are hard to draw) a change of the prosodic pattern of the word form is recorded, which manifests itself in different syllables receiving durational prominence: kuniikaŋ 'you do / he does' — məkkuunikaŋ 'we (du.) do' — tkujaanikaŋəŋ 'I want to do'. There are no phonologically significant tones in Kerek.
new_statements.citation: Володин, А. П. 1997. Керекский язык. In: А. П. Володин (отв. ред.), Языки мира: Палеоазиатские языки, pp. 53–60. Москва: Индрик. ISBN 5-85759-046-9.
new_statements.locator: p. 54, §5.1.0 'Фонологические сведения' (second paragraph, end) and §5.1.1 'Слоговая организация слова'
new_statements.rule_in_words: Volodin does not state a stress position for Kerek in its own right: he says the word-level prosody follows the general Chukotko-Koryak pattern and refers the reader to the Chukchi article in the same volume, and he reports that prominence is realized as vowel lengthening whose position shifts between syllables in individual idiolects (the three examples he gives all lengthen the second syllable from the left — ku-NII-kaŋ, mək-KUU-ni-kaŋ, tku-JAA-ni-ka-ŋəŋ — with the lengthened syllable falling on different morphemes; that second-syllable regularity is my observation, not his claim). Length is non-phonemic and there are no tones. The cross-referenced Chukchi rule is not in the saved file; our catalog's Chukchi entry (Dunn 1999) has primary stress on the first C-initial full-vowel syllable, and Alutor (Kibrik et al. 2000) stress on the first or second syllable, never on Cə.
new_statements.exceptions: Idiolectal variation only: 'in the idiolects of individual Kereks... different syllables receive durational prominence'; Volodin explicitly warns that broader conclusions are hard to draw (data from the last three speakers, 1991).
new_statements.domain_note: Word form (словоформа); §5.1.1 adds that the lengthened vowels are never split by a syllable boundary (мэк-куу-ни-каӈ) and that 'according to preliminary data there are grounds to speak of the prosodic organization not only of the word form but of the whole sentence (or a period of connected text)'. Inflected verb forms, not citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: Volodin 1997 describes Kerek as a whole (kere1280); his data come from the last three speakers (1991), whom the lingsib page assigns to the Navarin (2) and Khatyrka (1) dialects; the read pages do not name the dialect. Volodin treats Kerek as possibly one of the tribal languages/dialects of the Koryak community with strong Chukchi features. No dialect glottocodes exist.

sources.citation: Endangered Languages of Siberia project (IEA RAS), Kerek page + bibliography, http://lingsib.iea.ras.ru/ru/languages/kerek.shtml and /ru/bibliography/kerek.shtml
sources.note: Nothing on stress; says Kerek has fewer phonemes than its relatives and no vowel harmony; 3 speakers in 1991 (2 Navarin dialect, 1 Khatyrka). Bibliography lists Skorik 1968; Asinovskij & Volodin 1991 (manuscript, c. 20 a.l.); Volodin 1991 prospectus; Volodin 1997; Volodin 1994a (Красная книга, pp. 30–31); Volodin 1994b; Leont'ev 1983; Bogoraz 1934; Dall 1870.

en: phoneme inventory only (5 vowels per Fortescue 2005; consonants and vowels may be long), no stress statement; ru: no phonology section; ru bibliography adds Муравьёва, БРЭ 2009; Володин 2002 (Языки народов России: Красная книга, pp. 90–93); Леонтьев 1976.
